title: Where are you going?
goal: Master all six place endings at once in a single table — the core of the whole Finnish case system, and the part that suddenly makes fifteen cases make sense.
bekal: build the six place endings: *-ssa/-sta/-Vn* and *-lla/-lta/-lle*

notes: **Missä, mistä, mihin** — one word, three directions. All three are *mi-* with a different place ending. The same pattern sticks to any noun: *Helsingi**ssä*** (in), *Helsingi**stä*** (from), *Helsinki**in*** (to). Once you see it, you don't need to memorize any more lists — you just attach the ending.

**Tampereelle, not Tampereeseen.** Some Finnish towns take the "outer" set of endings instead of the "inner" one. These really have to be memorized, but luckily the list is short: *Tampere*, *Vantaa*, *Rovaniemi*, *Seinäjoki*, *Riihimäki*, and a handful more. The rest use the "inner" set: *Helsinkiin*, *Turkuun*, *Ouluun*.

**Junalla, bussilla, autolla** — means of transport take the ending *-lla/-llä*. Literally "on the train", which makes sense if you picture climbing onto something — English says "on the bus" too. The exception is *jalan* (on foot), a frozen form that never changes.
**Netistä** = *netti* + *-stä*. Note the gradation: two *t*'s become one. You buy something "from" the internet, where English says "online" or "on the internet".

**Kiitos vinkistä** — thanking uses the "from" ending. *Kiitos avu**sta*** (thanks for the help), *kiitos kahvi**sta***, *kiitos kaike**sta*** (thanks for everything). English says "for"; Finnish says "from".

**Tähän pysäkille** — two direction endings in one phrase, both meaning "to". *Tähän* comes from *tämä*, *pysäkille* from *pysäkki*. Even the pointing word changes form to match its noun, just like an adjective.

grammars.title: Six place endings — the core of the whole system
body: This is the most important table in the whole course. Finnish divides "place" into two sets — **inner** and **outer** — and each has three directions: staying in, coming from, going to. Six endings, one layout.
after: **The inner set is for containers and enclosed spaces**: house, room, shop, bag, country, city. **The outer set is for surfaces and open places**: table, floor, station, bus stop, beach, market. Most can be guessed by picturing the shape.

⚠️ **People always take the outer set.** *Ainolla on kirja* (Aino has a book), *annan kirjan Aino**lle*** (I give the book to Aino), *sain kirjan Aino**lta*** (I got the book from Aino). This is the use you'll need most every day, and it has nothing to do with place at all.

What can't be guessed and must be memorized: some town names (*Tampereella*), some countries (*Venäjällä* = in Russia, outer set), and some things (*torilla* = at the market, *kadulla* = on the street, but *kaupassa* = in the shop).

grammars.title: Building the "into" ending
body: Five of the six place endings are easy: you just attach them. Only "into" needs its own rule, because its shape depends on the base word.
after: ⚠️ **The "into" ending uses the STRONG grade.** *Kauppa → kaupassa* (weak) but *kauppa → kauppaan* (strong). It is the only place ending that doesn't weaken the consonant, and it often makes beginners hesitate. The rule of thumb: if you're going in, the consonant stays whole.
Words in *-i* whose stem changes to *-e-* follow the rule too: *Suomi → Suome- → Suomeen*, *nimi → nime- → nimeen*.

For *koti* (home, the place you return to) there are frozen forms you must learn: *kotona* (at home), *kotoa* (from home), *kotiin* (home, homeward). None of the three follows any pattern, and you'll use all three every day.

blocks.text: ⚠️ *Mennä* and *tulla* work from opposite points of view, just like English *go* and *come*: *menen* = I go away from here, *tulen* = I come toward you. If a friend invites you to their home, the right answer is *tulen*, not *menen* — because you are moving toward them.

blocks.text: Notice the pair *oikealle* (to the right) and *oikealla* (on the right) — the direction endings work exactly as you have just learned. The same goes for *vasemmalle* and *vasemmalla*.

blocks.title: Three place words you'll use every day
items: *tuolla* (over there, in sight) — *tuolta* (from over there) — *tuonne* (to over there)
These three rows follow the same six-ending pattern; their shapes have just frozen. Learn them as one group, not nine separate words.
